interactions.summary: Jiang escalates the Brutus-Cassius discussion into a larger interpretive claim that Virgil, not Lucifer, is the real master of hell, then quizzes the class about whether Dante's reliance on Virgil amounts to temptation and what allegory governs the climb into light.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang leading with short student answers

speaker_notes.note: The one-word student answer identifies Virgil as the implied master of hell in Jiang's framing.

claims.claim: Jiang argues that the placement of Brutus and Cassius implies that Virgil, not Lucifer, is the real power organizing hell in the poem's deeper logic.
Jiang treats the end of Inferno as a shock reveal in which the apparent ruler, Lucifer, turns out not to be the true guiding force behind the journey.
A student says Dante does trust Virgil despite intermittent doubts, and Jiang uses that trust as evidence that the temptation has already taken hold.
Jiang reads Dante riding on Virgil's back while they climb from darkness into sunlight as an allegorical setup whose meaning is still being tested through class guesses.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns the end of Inferno into a Hollywood-style reveal: Lucifer looked like the boss, but Virgil was the real operator all along.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It compresses Jiang's most provocative reinterpretation of Virgil's role and sets up the guide-as-tempter line that carries into Purgatorio.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's cinematic label for the poem's hidden reversal in which Virgil appears as the deeper power behind hell's logic.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture moves from explaining Brutus and Cassius's punishment to a broader reinterpretation of Virgil as the real tempter and hidden ruler of the infernal journey.

uncertainty_notes.note: The class proposes competing allegories before Jiang lands the interpretation, so the packet records a live interpretive search rather than settled consensus.
